items.title: Chink Martin Interview, 1966-10-19
items.q: The name 'Bailey' appears only in the interviewer's turn ('Ringling Brothers, Barnum and Bailey version') and is not mentioned by the interviewee or linked to any personal interaction.

ctx.x: That's right. The bass man is the only one making dum ba dum ba dum. And I will say it brought forth the best of the bass. The drum player is making a ribbit. The bum bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing. That's not helping the rhythm at all. Yeah. Oh well. Well, I guess that's it. How were the tempos in the old times? Did they play everything so fast? No, the old tempos was mediocre. That's what I learned.…

That's what I was telling you one other time, Tink, you may remember, why I kind of differentiate between what some people think of as Dixieland today and what we think of New Orleans jazz, all this fast stuff that they call Dixieland today, that's what I say, that's the Ringling Brothers, Barnum and Bailey version of New Orleans jazz.

That's not the real New Orleans jazz. No, we played, what was that affair that we played when we got, when all the actors and that came out, was it a hard fun or whatever it was? When we played with the band?
